name: Lega, Beya dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Botne, Robert. 2003. Lega (Beya dialect) (D25). In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages (Routledge Language Family Series), 422-449. London & New York: Routledge.
catalog_quote: [p. 425, 2.4 Vowel length] Vowels are lengthened in the penultimate syllable of a word in phrase-final position, as in [nákārį̄lē ŋkuːsu] 'I trapped a grey parrot'. However, if there is a high tone on the final vowel, lengthening does not occur, as, e.g. in [nákārį̄lē kapusú] 'I trapped a fisherman'. [pp. 426-427, 2.8 Tone] Lega is a tone language, having the following tones: H(igh), M(id) or downstepped H(igh), R(ising), F(alling) and L(ow). H and L are phonemically distinctive, as, apparently, is F in a few words. R and downstepped H tones are always derived, R from a combination of underlying L plus H. R and F may occur on short vowels. Mid tones pose a problem in that it is not clear whether they should be considered downstepped Hs. The environments for M and downstepped Hs are inadequately understood at this time, as it has not been possible to analyze tonal phenomena fully.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lega is a tone language (H vs L lexical contrast). The only prominence-like effect described is lengthening of the penultimate vowel of the word that stands in phrase-final position; this lengthening is suppressed when the word's final vowel carries a H tone. The chapter never speaks of stress or accent, and no word-level (non-phrase-final) prominence is described.
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate lengthening fails when the final vowel of the phrase-final word bears a high tone (e.g. kapusú 'fisherman'). Underlying long vowels exist independently (ideophones; kináaná 'eight', -kéeké 'small').
new_statements.domain_note: Phrase-level: lengthening applies to the penult of a word only in phrase-final position (examples are clause-final objects). Tone is lexical/grammatical; tonal analysis described by the author as incomplete. Variety: Beya (Kinyamunsange) dialect of Pangi District, Lega-Malinga.
new_statements.identity_note: Botne 2003 describes the Beya (also called Kinyamunsange) variety of Pangi District, a sub-variety of Lega-Malinga; Glottolog files this chapter under lega1249 Lega-Shabunda [lea], whose Ethnologue dialect list includes Kinyamunsange/Pangi, so identity with the target is good. Meeussen 1962/1971 describe the Banagabo variety recorded at Shabunda (also lega1249). Lungumbu 1988 describes Gonzabale of Mwenga District, which is more likely Lega-Mwenga [lgm] (lega1251). Botne notes Isile (Lega-Ntara) vs Lega-Malinga have only c. 67% lexical similarity.

tone_statements.citation: Masumbuko-wa-Busungu (1979). Esquisse Grammaticale du Lega. Bukavu: Institut Supérieur Pédagogique.
tone_statements.quote: Nous regrettons cependant d’avoir écrit les mots lega de ce livre sans y avoir mis les accents liés à la tonalité, cet aspect de la prosodie de cette langue. Cette lacune passagère sera comblée dans les éditions ultérieures.
tone_statements.translation: We regret, however, having written the Lega words of this book without adding the accents linked to tonality, that aspect of the prosody of this language. This temporary gap will be filled in later editions.

sources.note: No use of the words stress/accent/prominence anywhere in the chapter. Sect. 2.4 (p.425): vowels are lengthened in the penultimate syllable of a word in phrase-final position, but not if the final vowel bears a H tone. Sect. 2.8 (pp.426-427): Lega is a tone language, H and L phonemically distinctive, M/downstepped H, R, F (mostly) derived; tonal phenomena 'inadequately understood'.
